text: Finding product associations in transaction data
Ashwin A  ·  E0324097     |     Nikilesh J R  ·  E0324098
Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research
Project presentation for ADA23IN101. The application analyzes transaction baskets and surfaces association rules.
A transaction is a set of products purchased together in one basket.
Find recurring product combinations and express them as readable rules, such as {A, B} → {C}.
Merchants can use associations to explore merchandising, cross-sell ideas, and promotion hypotheses.
Output: frequent itemsets, association rules, and standard strength measures
Association mining describes co-occurrence in historical baskets. It does not establish why a customer bought a product.
Retail transaction logs can contain many baskets and distinct products.
Product relationships are difficult to inspect in raw rows.
Frequent pairs may be common simply because each product sells often.
Analysts need support, confidence, and lift thresholds to rank candidate rules.
The application reports measures as filters and ranking signals, not causal evidence.
References [1], [2], [3], and [5] are listed on slide 17.
Ingest and inspect transaction data from CSV or Excel.
Clean records and form transaction-level baskets.
Mine frequent itemsets with Apriori or FP-Growth.
Generate, filter, save, review, and export association rules.
The application describes co-occurrence in supplied transaction history. It does not perform sales forecasting, customer segmentation, causal inference, or measure actual revenue impact.
Results depend on data quality, basket definitions, and thresholds.
Saved analysis results support later review and CSV export.

Basket representation
Each transaction becomes a set of present products. Duplicate transaction-product pairs are removed during cleaning.

Mining choices
Apriori expands candidate itemsets. FP-Growth compresses baskets into a frequent-pattern tree.
Share of all baskets containing both sides
Share of A baskets that also contain B
Association strength relative to baseline B frequency
Measure definitions follow association-analysis literature [1,5,6]. The measures describe observed co-occurrence, not causality.
